BayesR3

 

BayesR3 takes a minimum of one command line argument, <parameter_file>:

 

%> bayesR3 <parameter_file>

 

 

The parameter file

 

The parameter file argument gives the name of a file used to pass a set of run time parameters as shown in Figure 1. The format uses a name (id) value style of input:

 

 -<command id>  <command value>  [optional command comment]

 

Note the ‘minus’ character in front of the command id. In the parameter file there is just one parameter per line specified and the line order of the parameters is not important.  The parameter file can also contain blank lines and comment lines. A black line is a line that only contains a carriage return, while a comment line is a line that begins with double forward slash ‘//’ as shown in Figure 1. All lines beginning with ‘//’ or are blank are simply skipped.

 

Command lines are identified by the lines beginning with a minus sign.  After this the command identifier name is specified, which is then followed by its value(s). Some commands can take 1 or more values and for such commands, a comma separated list of values is expected. Note in a comma separated list of values no spaces are expected, all values are on one line and there is no limit to the number of values allowed. For example:

 

-pi 0.94,0.049,0.01,0.001

 

Notice also in Figure 1 that individual commands can also contain comments. However, command comments must be all on one line following its command. If they go across lines each line must begin with //.  Also note that in this example,  Figure 1, each command comment starts with a double forward slash (//). However, on a command line the double slashes are optional.  All that is really required is a space separating the command value from the command comment. A detailed explanation of each command is given in Table 1.

 

Figure 1: Example parameter file. Notice comments after each parameter. In this example each comment starts with a double forward slash (//). A comment on each line is optional however the double slashes is just a matter of choice. All that is required is a space followed by some text after each parameter value.

 

Command line parameters

BayesR3 also takes separate command line arguments.  Command line options will override the parameters specified in the parameter file. Command line options, follow the same rules as applied to the parameter file other than command line arguments are not expected to contain comments:

 

Usage: bayesR3 <parameterFile>  [optional parameters]

           <parameterFile>  The name of a file containing a list of parameters

  Optional parameters:

           -L 0  if 1 then redirect screen output to a logfile is off. Default is zero

           -s <seed>: random number seed(s). Default is as a seed_seq of 61 integers generated C++'s random_device

           -genf <filename> name of genotype file

           -parts <0 or 1 or NA>. If 1 consider genotype file name as a file prefix

           -phef <filename> name of phenotype file

           -grm <filename> name of GRM file

           -fixf <filename> name of fixed effects file

           -classf <filename> name of SNP classification file

           -ref <filename> name of Reference set file

           -valid <filename> name of Validation set file

           -path <path> directory path for output files

           -pre <value> output file prefix

           -d <value> output detail; 1 = means only, 2 = full output, 3 collect SNP variances

           -ped <file name> name of pedigree file

           -I <value> number of iterations

           -burn <value> number of iterations for burn in

           -bs <value> block size must be a positive integer number

           -thin <value> thinning rate

           -pi <comma values> mixture model proportions eg: 0.95,0.04,0.02,0.01

           -alloc <comma values> mixture model allocations eg: 0.0,0.01,0.1,1

           -alpha <comma values> mixture model Dirichlet priors

           -h <comma values> trait heritability (h^2) values. One value for each trait to analyse

           -maf <value> //Minimum allele frequency

           -wtc <comma values> trait weight columns in the phenotype file

           -sc <value> scale and centre genotypes. Zero represents no scaling while 1 represents scaling

           -tc <comma values> trait column(s) to analyse

           -fext <type> output file extension types csv = comma separated, txt = space separated

           -DAV <0 or 1> if 1 determine additive genetic variance from data with flat priors

                     if 0 estimate it from the traits and heritability

           -force <0 or 1> if 1, then for multi-traits all SNP are considered to be associated

           -show Check and show input parameters and exit without running the analysis

           -chains <value> an integer value greater than or equal to 1

           -timing <comma values> run time analysis

           -drop <value> or NA. A positive integer value, used to control the dropping rate of SNPs. NA specifies no dropping

           -plusAlpha <0 or 1 or NA>. Specifies to add count of dropped SNPs to the alpha distribution

 

 

 

 

 

Detailed specification for these command options are given in Table 1.

 

Table 1: Explanation of command line arguments.

Parameter

Description

-L

The -L flag specifies that all standard output (that which usually gets printed on the screen) is saved to a log file. The suffix ‘log’ is appended to the output filename prefix, stored in the output path. This file can be viewed “live” using the tail command under Linux:

 

  tail -f -n +1 <output_path>/test.log.txt

 

 or via the powershell under windows:

 

        Get-Content -Path "output_path\test.log.txt" -Wait

 

To exit tail or Get-Content, at the command line, press the <ctrl>c keys simultaneously, where <ctrl> represents the control key.

-genf

Used to specify the genotype filename. Filename can include a directory path and the file can be a .gz file.  A filename can also be a split prefix name, this prefix should only be part of the split subpart files. See:

 Split genotype files: genotype file prefix

 

-parts

If 1 then treat the genotype file names as a prefix name, otherwise the genotype file name represents a single file.

Default value is 0

-phef

Used to specify the phenotype filename. Filename can include a directory path and the file can be a .gz file.

-ped

An optional pedigree file that contains three columns: animal ID, sire ID, dam ID in this order.  Default is NA.

 

This file can be a .gz file.

The IDs can be either numeric or alphanumeric. Zero is used to represent a missing sire or dam.  It is desirable that the pedigree file should also contain the non-genotyped ancestors of the genotyped animals as these ancestors provide links between families.

-grm

An optional genetic relationship matrix file, which contains a nxn matrix of record relationships as determined by their SNPs. Or it can be an A-matrix as determined from a pedigree. The value of n must be at least as large as the number of phenotypes to be analyzed or larger. This file is expected to contain n+1 columns. Where the first column gives the record IDs. There is no specified order of the records required.

 

Default is NA.

 

This file can be a .gz file.

The IDs can be either numeric or alphanumeric and must match to those specified in the phenotype, genotype and fixed effects file.

-fixf

Used to specify the fixed effects filename. Filename can include a directory path and the file can be a .gz file.

-ref

Name of a file containing a list of reference ID’s. The animals/records specified in the reference set are used in the analysis. All other animals/records will be ignored. This file can be a .gz file.

-valid

Name of a file containing a list of validation ID’s. The animals/records specified in the validation set are used only in a predictBayeR3 analysis. All other animals/records will be ignored. This file can be a .gz file.

-classf

Name of a file containing a classification for each SNP. This file can be a .gz file.

-path

The path option is used to specify a directory where the output result files will be saved to. If the given path doesn’t exist, then it will be created. If the path contains a directory tree, then all directories along that path if needed will also be created.

--ppath

A directory path used by predictBayesR3 to store its results if set. Default is NA and in which case predictBayesR3 uses the directory defined by -path.

-pre

The prefix option is used to specify a leading common name for the output results files. Therefore, all result files will have the same starting prefix. The prefix can also contain a leading directory path. However, if this path doesn’t exist it won’t be created, and an error will be generated.

-s

The -s flag specifies an optional seed for the random number generator. As all implemented statistical distributions used by bayesR3, such as the Dirichlet, Beta, Chi-squared, uniform and normal distributions, are deterministic, they have been configured to use the same random number generator engine to ensure that repeat runs with the same seed(s) on the same data will generate 100% the same output result sets.

 

For a multi-chain analysis, as only a single set of seed values can be specified therefore, the specified seed values will be divided into equal (if possible) seed sets for each chain. For multi chain analysis the number of seeds must be equal or greater than the number of chains.

 

If a seed is not specified, then a non-deterministic set of 61 seeds are used to seed the random number generator engine at program startup and which will be printed to screen or saved to the log file at run time. Therefore, a seed can be a single value, or a comma separated sequence of seed values such as:

 

bayesR3 <parameter_file> -s 101,1193,4283

 

NB:

·                  No spaces are allowed between the seed values. 

 

-d

The -d option is used to specify the level of output detail. If d is set to 1 then only the mean values are specified and only the mean SNP effects are collected and saved in the effects file. If d is set to 2 then, an extra file is created, and a trace of all the SNP effects per post-burn iteration is saved. The suffix “_SNPtrace” is appended to the file name for these results.

 

NB: the trace only includes the post burn in iteration results. To get every result at every iteration the burn in needs to be set to zero. The trace file will have (iterations - burn)/block_size rows by the #SNP columns. The order of the SNPs will be the same as in the genotype file.

-I

The number of iterations to perform.

-burn

The number of iterations to ignore. If this parameter isn’t set or set to NA, then it will automatically be set to half the number of iterations.

 

Default value NA

-chains

A chain represents a computer thread. Each chain also represents a replicated run. Therefore, specifying 3 chains implies that 3 sets of output files will be produced with file name suffices chn1, chn2, and chn3 being adding to each file in each output set.

Default value 1

-bs

Optional value. If set to NA or -1 (default value) then block size is determined

From , where #Records represents the number of records being analyzed.

 

If block size is set to zero, then a non-blocked Bayes R will be run.

 

For a blocked bayesR, the block size (ideally, should be a multiple division of the #SNPs). Determining the best block size can be a little difficult, but as a rule  if block size if left unspecified that is: -bs NA.

 

The following R function (findMod) can at times help:

N.B: The maximum block size should be no more than the square root of the number of records in the analysis.

 

 

 

-pi

Mixture proportions.  A comma separated list, where the number of values defines the number of mixture components and each value defines the starting value for each component (the first value is reserved for the zero component); For example: 0.95,0.03,0.01,0.01. Setting this value sets nd to equal the number of items in the list.

-alloc

Mixture allocations. List of values separated by commas, each representing the scaling factor for the variance of a mixture component. Note that the number of values should match that in -pi. Setting this value sets nd to equal the number of items in the list.

-alpha

Mixture Dirichlet priors. List of values separated by commas. Note that the number of values should match the number of mixture proportions. Setting this value sets nd to equal the number of items in the list.


-h

Trait heritabilities. A comma separated list of values. Each heritability value is a value between 0 and 1.  The order of these values are expected to match the order of the phenotype columns to be analyzed. That is, the first heritability corresponds to the first trait specified etc.

 

If the number of heritabilities = 1, and the number of traits is greater than 1, then the given heritability will be used for all traits.

 

-tc

trait column(s) in the phenotype file to analyze. A comma separated sequence of values from 1 to nc, where nc is the number of trait columns in the phenotype file. 1 is the first column after the animal id column in the phenotype file  for example:

 

   bayesR3 <parameter_file> -tc 5,6,7,21

 

specifies that columns 5, 6, 7 and 21 in the phenotype file are to be used for analysis. When more than one column is specified a bayesR3 multi-trait analysis is performed. 

 

Note: the number of traits to be analyzed must match the number of heritability values, unless the number of heritabilities is 1. In this case, the one heritability value specified is used for all traits.

-wtc

Weight column(s) in the phenotype file. A comma separated sequence of values from 1 to nw, where nw is the number of weight columns in the phenotype file. 1 represents the first column after the record id column. NA is used to specify no weight columns are specified. For multi-trait analysis, the wtc can specify just 1 column or a comma separated list of column numbers. If only one column is specified, then the weights in that column are used for all traits. If multiple columns are specified, then the number of weight columns specified must match the number of phenotype columns specified.

-sc

Scale and centre genotype data. 0 represents no scaling while 1 represents scaling

The elements of V, the genotype matrix data, are often coded as either 0, 1 or 2 for respective homozygote first/major allele, heterozygote and homozygote second/minor allele. Equivalently, they can be coded in terms of allelic dosages. The elements of V are normalized via:

 

 

Where  represents a coded allele, or an allelic dosage value, and  represents the frequency of the minor allele for SNP j,  represents the number of records and where i indexes across the records.

Default value 1

-fext

Specifies the output file extension types to be either csv or txt. Csv files are comma delimited, txt files are either space or tab delimited as summarized:

 

 

Type

Delimiter

File extension

cvs

comma

.csv

txt

space

.txt

tab

tab

.txt

For example:

 

   bayesR3 <parameter_file> -fext tab

 

Specifies a tab delimited output style and will result in text files with file prefix ‘.txt’.

Default value  csv

-DAV

If 1, determine the additive genetic variance from the data. If 0, estimate the additive genetic variance for each trait using its variance and given heritability value.

Default value 1

-force

If 1, then for multi-traits all SNPs are associated to all traits. For single trait analysis it has no effect. A forced multi-trait analysis is identical to a single trait analysis, for each trait analyzed.

Default value 0

-show

Used to check and show the input parameters. BayesR3 analysis will not be performed.

Default value 0

-timing

Only supported on single trait analysis. A comma separated sequence of integer values. The sequence of integers can contain 1 or more values, where each value specifies a block size, in any order. For example:

 

bayesR3 <parameter_file> -timing 0,3,7,11,27,48

 

Will perform a timing analysis for your single trait analysis. This will output a 4 column by 6 lines text file, with format as described by the file extension. Each output line will contain 4 columns, where the first column gives the block size, and following 3 columns will contain 3 replicate timings for each of the block sizes specified.

Default value NA

-drop

An optional integer value. NA, 0 or 0,0 are 3 ways to specify no dropping.

 

The drop parameter is used to drop SNPs from analysis that have probabilities of being included in the model.  Dropping only occurs during burn in.  The drop parameter takes 1 or 2 comma separated values. Default value is NA, which is used to specify no dropping.

 

For example:

 

-drop 100

 

Specifies that during burn in, a SNP will be dropped from analysis if in the last 100 iterations it was not included in the model. In this case dropping can only occur on and after the 100th iteration. 

 

-drop 100,200

 

Specifies that during burn in, a SNP will be dropped from analysis if in the previous 100 iterations it was not included in the model. In this case dropping starts at the 200th iteration.

 

-drop NA

 

Specifies no dropping.

-plusAlpha

Used in conjunction with -drop and is an optional value, which is one of the following values: 0, 1, or NA. If 0 or NA is specified, then -plusAlpha is off. If 1, then -plusAlpha is on. The default state is off.

 

Example usage:

 

-plusAlpha 1

 

If on, then BayesR3’s mixture counts for all dropped SNPs are added to the n Dirichlet alpha distribution, where n, usually set to 4, represents the number of mixtures in BayesR3’s Gaussian mixture model. BayesR3 does this by keeping track of the number of times each SNP falls into the 1st, 2nd, …, nth distribution.  Then, when a SNP is dropped, its distributional counts are normalized to sum to one and these normalized values get added to the corresponding Dirichlet prior alpha distribution values. The net effect is that SNPs get dropped at a faster rate than when plusAlpha  is off, and more SNPs will generally get pushed into higher distributional positions than when plusAlpha is off. This also means that some SNPs will get assigned larger effect values, which in turn can improve the prediction bias, but only if it’s below 1 when no dropping is specified. Therefore, when plusAlpha is on the actual bias value is expected to increase a few percentage points.

 

NB bayesR3 will issue a warning if -plusAlpha is on when dropping is off.

 

 

 

 

Version identification

 

 

BayesR3 uses the build date as its version identification. The build date is incorporated into bayesR3 prior to its release. The simplest way to get to the version identification is to call bayesR3 from the command line with no arguments and its build date will be displayed in the first line of the output:

 

> bayesR3

 

BUILD: Mar 16 2020 15:26:35

Usage: bayesR3 <parameterFile>  [optional parameters]

         <parameterFile>  The name of a file containing a list of parameters

….

 

 

 

The version identification is also included in the runtime output from bayesR3 and if the -L option is used and is set to 1 it will be saved in the log file for future reference.  Date stamps, the file creation time associated with the bayesR3 result output files can also be used, indirectly, to identify the release version of bayesR3 responsible for their creation.

 

The version identification can be used to check consistency between runs. It is possible upon request to get previous versions of the bayesR3 executable if needed, and if you know the date of when you ran your analysis.

 

Input files

 

All input files read by bayesR3 are space delimited plain ascii text files; Also, all input files other than the parameter file can be a ‘.gz’ compressed file.

 

As genotype files can be very large (100s of gigabytes or terabytes), it is worthwhile in terms of disk storage to have these files saved in compressed form. The left panel in Figure 2 shows an example of the compression ratio achieved with gzip on a typical but small genotype file, 716 records by 37008 SNPs. The right figure shows the time required to read these files line by line using either C++’s ifstream or by igzstream (a C++ interface to zlib).

 

To create a gzip file under windows: browse to the location where the file you want to compress is located. Right click on the text file name and select   7-Zip > Add to archive… From the pop-up window set the Archive format to gzip and then click the OK button to start compressing.

 

To create a gzip file under Linux use gzip. Example: $> gzip genofile.txt, this will result in the genofile.txt file being replaced by genofile.gz.

 

 

Figure 2: left panel gives the size of a .txt formatted genotype file to its compressed version (.gz). The right panel gives the read speed of these files, where S.txt is the read time of the .txt file using C++ ifstream, the G.txt result is for reading the .txt file using igzstream and the .gz result is from the .gz file being read using igzstream.

 

The order of reading of the various files are:

 

1.     Pedigree file

2.     Reference set or Validation set

3.     Phenotype file

4.     Genotype file

5.     Fixed effects file

6.     Classification file

 

If there is a reference set specified for analysis, then the IDs in this file will determine which records are read from the phenotype file, genotype file and fixed-effects file. If there is no refence set provided, then the IDs in the phenotype file determines which records from the genotype and fixed-effects files are to be included in the analysis. The order of rows in each of these files don’t need to be the same. BayesR3 will align them automatically using the ID’s given separately in each file.

 

If a pedigree file is specified, then the pedigree file is handled differently. All pedigree information is read in to create a relationship matrix. After which, it is reduced in size, prior to analysis, to only include the records as determined by the reference file or by the phenotype file.

 

The validation file is used only by predictBayesR3, see below, and is ignored by bayesR3.

 

 

 

Phenotype file

A phenotype file (see Table 2) is a space delimited text file (txt), with no header line. All the phenotype data for a record should be presented on one line. The file should contain a minimum of at least two columns; The first column (column 0) should contain the record IDs. Subsequent columns should contain the phenotypes (traits) for each record, and any corresponding weights.

 

Individual phenotype (trait) values for any record can be missing. Missing values should be denoted by a ‘*’, a ‘.’ or by the character string ‘NA’. Internally, missing values are handled by setting a zero weight for that missing value otherwise a weight of 1 is used for all non-missing values.

 

BayesR3 doesn’t expect or specify any ordering of the trait or weight columns in the phenotype file. Other than they must appear after the ID column, which must be the first column in the file. The user specifies, via the parameter file or via the command line, which columns in the phenotype file are to be considered as the trait columns for analysis, and which columns, if any, are the weight columns. It’s not an error to specify the same trait column multiple times. The phenotype file can contain more trait and weight columns than those specified for analysis.

 

With respect to the weight columns and for multi-trait analysis, weights can be specified in the parameter file by either:

1.     NA in which case there are no user specified weights to include

2.     Specifying a single value and in this case the weights in this column will be used as the weights for each trait to be analyzed

3.     Specifying a comma list of weight columns. The order and the number of the given weight columns are expected to coincide with the order and number of traits given for the trait columns to analyze; that is, the first weight column will be associated to the first trait column specified in the parameter file and so on.

Genotype file

This file is also a space delimited text file with no header line. All the genotype data for a record should be presented on one line. The line (row) order of the genotype file does not need to match the order given in the phenotype file. Only those lines corresponding to records specified in the phenotype file or via a reference file (see below) will be extracted and used in the analysis. All phenotype records to be analyzed need to match uniquely to one genotype record.

 

The genotype file should contain at least two columns; the first column should contain the record ID. A genotype file containing n SNPs would therefore, contain (n+1) columns.

 

Missing genotypes are designate in the genotype file by the same codes as used for the phenotype file. That is a period(.), an asterix (*) or NA. Missing genotypes will be replaced by the mean genotype value for the given marker. If a SNP column is completely full of missing values, it’s values will be set to 0 and it will get flagged as a monomorphic SNP, and hence ignored during further analysis.

 

1.     The genotype for each SNP is entered as a code where 0 = 1 1, 1 = 1 2 or 2 1 and 2 = 2 2. In this case 0, 1 or 2 are the only values expected for each genotype value in each SNP column.

2.     Genotypes can also be represented in terms of allelic dosages as shown in Table 3.

Split genotype files: genotype file prefix

 

As genotype files can be very large requiring bayesR3 to spend many hours just to load a terabyte genotype file, bayesR3 has the feature that it can read genotype files in parallel, thereby greatly speeding up the read time required.  However, the file must be split into small parts (see below) and the –parts command must be turned on.

 

 

If the -parts command is on then just pass to bayesR3 via the -genf command the output prefix used to split the original genotype file into parts, using the UNIX split command (or equivalent, such as with Windows power-shell):

 

 

zcat subSet4e4.txt.gz | split - -l10000 subParts4e4

 

split options used:

-        get input from stdin

-l    break up by line

subparts4x4 file prefix name

 

For a genotype file containing 65,000 records/lines the above linux split command will generate the following 7 files:

 

subParts4e4aa subParts4e4ab subParts4e4ac subParts4e4ad subParts4e4ae subParts4e4af subParts4e4ag

 

Each containing 10,000 records/lines except for the last file (subParts4e4ag), which will contain only 5,000 records/lines. In this case the filename is passed to bayesR3 is:

 

-genf  ./pathToFile/subParts4e4

 

For example:

 

Run with original file:

 

Reading genotype(s) from ../../Iona/Geno/subSet4e4.txt

Time to load genotypes: 171.113(sec)

genotype (rows,cols) = 41925,40000

 

Run using split sub parts:

 

Reading genotype(s) from ../../Iona/Geno/subParts4e4aa

Reading genotype(s) from ../../Iona/Geno/subParts4e4ag

Reading genotype(s) from ../../Iona/Geno/subParts4e4ad

Reading genotype(s) from ../../Iona/Geno/subParts4e4ae

Reading genotype(s) from ../../Iona/Geno/subParts4e4ab

Reading genotype(s) from ../../Iona/Geno/subParts4e4ac

Reading genotype(s) from ../../Iona/Geno/subParts4e4af

Time to load genotypes: 49.0261(sec)

genotype (rows,cols) = 41925,40000

 

 

This equates to 3.5 times speed up. The greater the number of cores and split parts the faster the read will be. Also note the order of the file reading doesn’t matter.

 

To split and zip the genotype file in one step use:

 

zcat subSet4e4.txt.gz | split  -  -l10000 --filter='gzip > $FILE.gz' subParts4e4

 

An equivalent PowerShell command for file splitting by lines is:

 

$i=0; Get-Content subSet4e4.txt -ReadCount 10000 | %{$i++; $_ | Out-File sub4e4.$i }

 

Note:

·                 do not split a .gz file. Ungzip it first.

·                 the prefix should not be part of any other file name in the   directory holding the split subpart files and or genotype file.

 

Pedigree file

This file is also a space delimited text file, where the first three columns (see Table 4); are expected to represent animal ID, sire ID and dam ID and in that order. However, if the pedigree file has more than 3 columns only the first 3 columns are read.

 

Zero is used to represent a missing sire or dam. Therefore, it follows that no animal can have an ID of zero. The order of the rows is expected to be such that oldest animals/organisms precede the youngest; that is, parents come before offspring.

 

To keep the pedigree file as small as possible, the pedigree file should contain only those animals specified in the phenotype file and their relatives. This can be achieved via Phil’s distilPedigree program.

The population described in the pedigree can include IDs with rec-ords to be analysed or IDs without records for analysis and therefore, these animals get excluded. This is done by constructing an ‘A-matrix’. The A-matrix can be conceptualised as 4 blocks:

 

 

Theses 4 blocks (sub-matrices) specify the relationships between the excluded animals  and the included  (animals or plants to be analysed). BayesR3 extracts the sub-matrix  and then inverts it to produce ,  which is the inverse pedigree relationship matrix of the included records, and this is the matrix that gets included into the analysis.

 

GRM (A-matrix) file

A genomic relationship matrix (GRM) is essentially equivalent to the A-matrix as described above; therefore, bayesR3 allows for the input of a GRM or an A-matrix file via the use of the “-grm” command. A GRM file or an A-matrix file is expected to be a space delimited file without any header line. It is also expected to contain a  matrix of record relationships as determined from some set of SNPs, or from some pedigree.  This GRM/A-matrix file is also expected to contain  columns, where the first column contains the record IDs as shown in Table 5.

 

The value of  must be at least as large as the number of phenotypes that will get included from the phenotype file for analysis. As bayesR3 does automated matching of records, the order of the rows (lines) doesn’t need to match the order given in the phenotype file. Therefore, there is no specified ordering of the GRM or A-matrix file other than the first column must contain the record IDs.

Reference file

This is an optional text file, and when specified it is expected to contain only the ID’s for the records to include in the analysis. The file is expected to contain a single column of IDs; that is, one ID per line. However, if the file contains multiple columns of text, then they are expected to be separated by spaces but only the first column of text is used as the identifying reference set.

 

The reference file is used to specify which records are to be included in the current analysis of bayesR3.

 

Validation file

Validation files are used only in predictBayesR3, where if specified in the parameter file the validation file is used to specify which entries to be included for analysis by predictBayesR3. Its format is as specified for the reference file.

 

Fixed effects file

This file is also a space delimited text file (see Table 6). All the fixed effects data for a record should be presented on one line. This file is a design matrix allocating records to fixed effects. The first column contains the record IDs. Subsequent columns specify the fixed effects associated with each ID.

If a fixed effects file is specified, once it’s read and its rows have been matched up according to the reference file or phenotype file, each column in the resulting fixed effects matrix, except for the intercept column, are checked for variance. Any columns where the minimum and maximum coefficients are equal will be automatically excluded from the analysis and the effects for these columns will be set to zero in the output.

 

 

Classification file

 

This is an optional space delimited file that contains no header line. This file allows SNPs to be classified into two or more groupings, where each classification group is assigned its own mixture model. The initial mixture model assigned to each group is defined as the mixture model specified in the parameter file, and or specified on the command line.

 

A classification file contains a list of the SNPs as specified in the genotype file together with their classification. The order (line-order) of SNPs in this file is the same as the order (column-order) in the genotype file. Therefore, the number SNPs in the classification must match the number of SNPs given in the genotype file. An example of some entries from a classification file is shown in Table 8.

 

The file must contain only four columns in the following order:

1.     Alpha numeric SNP ID. This is just unique identify. Here it used to encode the chromosome and SNP position on that chromosome.

2.     Chromosome number.

3.     Base pair position within chromosome.

4.     SNP classification. Classifications should be numeric, consecutive (i.e. no gaps between classifications) and numbered from 1 to the number of classifications.

Output files

 

Output file names

BayesR3 can output up to 8 types of files (as summarised in Table 9) and the names of the output files are constructed in the following manner:

 

<path>/<filePrefix>_<suffix>[.chnX].<txt|csv>

 

where <filePrefix> is the output file prefix provided in the parameter file. The suffix is determined by bayesR3 and is used to assign and distinguish various output results as described in Table 9. The `.chnX’ extension is only used when the number of chains specified by the user is greater than 1. The designation X represents a number from 1 to N, where N is the number of chains specified. Therefore, if 3 chains are specified then 3 sets of output files will be generated, one from each chain. Each chain set of files represents replicate runs, each seeded with a different set of  nondeterministic random seed values.

 

Table 9: Output file descriptions summaries. See documentation for more detail information on each output file

Suffix

Description

Effects

Gives the SNP effects and posterior inclusion probabilities (discussed below)

Model

Contains posterior samples of the model parameters and the fixed effects (discussed below)

Poly

Contains the effects due to the pedigree

log

A log file of the runtime parameters, command line and standard output produced by bayesR3 (discussed below)

SNPtrace

File(s) containing a trace of all SNP effects (discussed below)

yhat

Gives the predicted y-values obtained from the model. It can be considered the average value of the response variable given the input matrices and the determined effects.

Timings

Gives a text file which contains a set of timing results, see Table 1.

aveEffects

From a multi-chain analysis. The SNP effects and their distribution proportions from each chain are collected averaged and stored in the aveEffects file. The SNP effects results will also be stored along with their variance across the chains.

 

 

 

The Effects file

The suffix ‘_Effects’ is appended to the output.  The effects file will have a row for each SNP and the SNP row order, on output, will be the same as SNP column order found in genotype input file (see Table 10). For monomorphic SNPs, although they are excluded from the analysis, in the Effects file their associated rows will contain all zeros.

 

This file is a user specified delimited file that contains the mean posterior estimates for each individual SNP. The column labelled Freq gives the frequency for the minor allele for each SNP. The column labelled Beta gives the SNP mean effect, and the posterior inclusion probabilities of the SNP effect in the mixture classes 1 to k, are identified by the column headers PIP1, …, PIPK. For example, Table 10  shows that the first SNP, has a 71 % probability that its coefficient -88.6885, falls in the fourth distribution (PIP4).

For multi-trait analysis the effects file layout is slightly different, as shown in Table 11.  It still has a row for each SNP effect, and the order is the same as the order given in the genotype file. However, it has a set of PIP and Beta columns for each trait analyzed, with the trait number appended to the column headers. The trait number reflects the order in which the trait columns were entered. For example, for trail columns specified as: “-tc 6,5”, trait 1 refers to trait column 6, and trait 2 is referring to trait column 5.

 

It also contains two Q columns, where Q1 gives the unassociated probability of the SNPS, while Q2 gives the associated probability for each SNP. If a SNP is deemed unassociated, it signifies that it has no effect on any of the traits analyzed for that SNP.  These columns help in determining if a SNP is jointly contributing to the analyzed traits.

The Model file

The suffix ‘_Model’ is appended to the output prefix<id>. This file will contain a column for each trait analyzed in the order of the trait-columns specified in the parameter file or via the command line. This file is also used to hold the classification class proportions for each group specified in the classification file.

 

Each column other than the first and those columns associated with the last N-lines of this file, which are used to hold the grouping classification proportions (see below), and N is the number of classification groups, will contain: 

 

1.     R^2, which gives the goodness of fit for the model to the data analyzed

2.     Mean, the model intercept

3.     Vp, the trait/phenotype variance of the input data

4.     Va the genetic variance explained by the SNPs

5.     Ve the residual variance

6.     Vg the variance of the genetic effects explained by the pedigree (if specified)

7.     Vyhat the variance of the yhats.

8.     nMono the number of monomorphic SNPs detected, as specified according to the minimum allele frequency given in the parameter file

9.     Associated gives the number of SNPs considered to be associated with the model. For single trait analysis this will include all the SNPs minus the monomorphic SNPs

10.  nSNPs the number of SNPs considered to be in the model for that trait

11.  Nk1, …, Nkk, gives the number of SNPs detected to be in the mixture components 1 to k

12.  Pk1, …, Pkk, the proportion of the SNPs in the mixture components 1 to k

13.  Vk1, …, Vkk are the sum of squares of the SNP effects in the mixture components 1 to k

14.  F1, …, Fn gives the fixed effects, if any; where, F1 will give the fixed effect for the 1st effect in the fixed effects file, F2 the 2nd and so on. Note F1 if present will be a replication of the Mean row

15.  VF1, …, VFn, gives the variances associated with each fixed effect.

Classification distributions

 

If a classification file has been specified and the analysis performed was a single trait analysis, then, for a single trait analysis, the last 2N lines, N being the number of classification groups, in the model file will contain the distribution counts for the SNPs with respect to their classification are given as shown below:

 

 

 

 

Consider just Class 1:

The numbers in the first square brackets [1.9e+02,0.17,0.38,41], represents the number of SNPs falling into each of 4 distributions (1,2,3,4) during the post-burn-in analysis. The numbers in the 2nd square brackets [1, 1, 1, 1] represent the alpha distribution. The first number, 233, past the alpha distribution represent the number of SNPs assigned to that class minus the number of monomorphic SNPs in that class. The next number, 41.26, is the sum of the SNPs falling into distributions 2, 3 and 4. The zero at the end is the sum of values in the alpha distributions minus the number of distributions. This will usually be zero unless SNPs have been dropped during analysis.

 

 

The Poly file

 

The suffix ‘_Poly’ is appended to the output prefix<id>. This is an optional file, which will only be produced if a pedigree or GRM file is specified in the parameter file or via the command line. It will contain 2 or more columns, one column for each trait analyzed. These columns contain the pedigree polygenetic effects for each record analyzed (Table 13)

The Log file

The suffix ‘_log’ is appended to the output prefix<id>. This is an optional file, which will only be produced if the command line option -L is used (see Table 1). It will contain run time information about the results being generated; such as parameter settings, the random number seed used, the variances, how long the bayesR3 will run etc. An example of the runtime output is given in the Appendix.

 

The SNPtrace file

 

The suffix ‘_SNPtrace’ is appended to the output prefix<id>. This is an optional file, which will only be produced if output detail or -d command line option is set to 2. This will produce a large file, with the number of columns equal to the number of SNPs in the genotype file by the number of rows equal to the number of iterations minus the burn in iterations. This file will be written to disk as a compressed gzip file. The information in this file is useful to see if the SNP effects have converged over the burn in period.

 

The yhat file

The suffix ‘_yhat’ is appended to the output prefix<id>. This file gives the predicated trait values, it will contain a minimum of two columns, the first column will give the associated IDs, this will be followed by columns of yhat values, one column for each trait analyzed. The order of the yhat columns, will match the order of traits given in the parameter file, or given in the -tc command line option (see Table 14).

PredictBayesR3

 

PredictBayesR3 is used to do 3 things: validations, predictions and correlations and it takes a minimum of one command line argument, <parameter_file>:

 

%> predictBayesR3 <parameter_file>

 

It is designed to run using the same input parameters as passed to BayesR3. either by a parameter file or on the command line, but after the associated BayesR3 run. If the input and output files specifications use absolute addresses than predictBayesR3 can be run from any directory. Otherwise, it should be run from the same directory BayesR3 was run from.  

 

If the parameter -L is set to 1 then predictBayesR3’s output, which gets printed to standard out (the screen), will get appended to the associated log file generated by BayesR3, if no associated log file was created by BayesR3 then predictBayesR3 will create one.

 

If the -ppath command is used to specify a directory path to be used by predictBayesR3, that by default is set to NA, will store all its output in this directory.  If the directory contains a Log file, and -L command is set to 1, then predictBayesR3 standard output will be appended to this file, otherwise if needed a log file will be created. This effectively gives predictBayesR3 its own log file.

 

At this stage predictBayesR3 doesn’t use the polygenetic effects that may have been produced by bayesR3.

 

 

Validation:

A validation is when the input parameters define a reference file, or a validation file, phenotype file and genotype file. When a validation file is used then all records specified in this file are included in the analysis. When only a reference file is used then all records in the phenotype file not included in the reference set are used to determine the model’s accuracy.  The output of a validation will be a <filename>_Valid_yhat text file, which will be placed in the output directory defined in the parameter file, and a R^2 value and a slope value will go to the screen or log file.

 

Correlation:

A correlation analysis is performed when the input parameters does not define a reference, or a validation, file but defines only a phenotype file and a genotype file. Then all the records in the genotype that match records in the phenotype files are used to perform a correlation between the modelled phenotypes to the actual phenotypes given in the phenotype file. The output of a correlation will be a <filename>_Valid_yhat text file, which will be placed in the output directory defined in the parameter file, and a R^2 value and a slope value will go to the screen or log file.

 

A correlation is generally used to make predictions using records that aren’t defined in the training phenotype file. This could be the case where you have trained on a certain breed/strain of animals or plants and want to see if you can predict into a different breed or strain. However, the genotype file supplied must contain entries for the entries supplied in the “new phenotype” file.  Example usage:

 

In the example above the fixed effects file is also turned off. This is only required if the new phenotype file doesn’t have entries in the fixed effect file.

 

Prediction:

A prediction is performed when the input parameters does not define a phenotype file but defines a genotype file. Here the genotype file is used to fit a set of predicted phenotypes. The output of a prediction will only be:  <filename>_Valid_yhat text file.

 

If a reference file is supplied, then the prediction is performed using the genotypes from records not defined in the reference file.

If a validation file is supplied all genotypes specified in the validation file are used for the predictions.

 

It is an error to define a fixed effect file without defining a phenotype file.

 

 

 

Appendix

 

Common errors encountered:

 

·                 Error: number of SNP rows in classification file NOT equal to number of SNP columns in …. file

o   Often bayesR3 or predictBayesR3 reports a miss match between the number of records in one input file with another. While this can be the case, sometimes it’s indicating there are duplicate record ID’s in one or more of the input files.

·                 Other common causes of problems:

o    The genotype or other input file not being a space separated file.

·                 Invalid parameter file

o   Check for missing or misspelt parameters in the parameter file.

Example slurm script

 

The following gives an example of a simple slurm script.

 

The memory required for the SNP analysis can be determined from:


 

Where #R is the number of records; #SNPS is the number of SNPS, #F is the number of fixed effects and Ped represents the elements required if a pedigree is included in the analysis where   ; BS is the block size and #T represents the number of traits which gets double to account for the weights associated with each trait.  Weights are used even if the user doesn’t specify any weight columns. In this case the weights are usually just 1 or 0, which account for any missing phenotypes.

 

The time is usually estimated from knowing the time required to analyze other similar sized data sets, or by running a timing analysis.

 

Chains and number of cores/threads (cpus-per-task):

The number of cores/threads should be at least 8, and for a multi-chain analysis no less than . However, the number 8 is somewhat arbitrary, as BayesR3 only needs 1 core per chain once it starts solving the genomic equations. Also, during startup BayesR3 processes several tasks in parallel if possible, such as loading genotype files, building blocks etc. For example, if you split the genotype file into 100 parts, then you might want to use 100 cores. If you want to run 10 chains, then set cores to 10 etc.

 

 

 

 

 

 

Multi-trait PCA values

 

The multi-trait analysis performed by bayesR3 assumes that traits are uncorrelated and if you can’t assume the traits are independent, then one way to ensure this is to run a PCA analysis on the traits. The following R function getPCAvalues can be used to generate a PCA file suitable for use as a phenotype file in a multi-trait bayesR3 analysis using a given bayesR phenotype file.

 

The resulting PCA file output is written to same directory that contains the original phenotype file, but with the file extension “.pca.txt”. Therefore, the input file name is expected to contain its directory path. The first output column in the PCA file will contain the record IDs specified in the original phenotype file, and the following columns will contain the PCA values from 1 to N, where N is the number of PCA components that explain for example 90% of the total variances in your data. The actual percentage is user determined and is set using the thresh parameter, and its default value is 0.9: 

 

 

 

 

Change log

 

 

     

·       Missing genotypes are now automatically detected and imputed.  The genotype codes for missingness are a period (.), an asterix (*) or NA. Missing genotypes will be replaced by the mean genotype value for the given marker.

·       Added new command switch -ppath, which if set, sets a directory path to be used by predictBayesR to write its results into and separately from bayesR3

·       Fixed problem with bayesR3 and predictBayesR3 not determining if a file opened correctly

·       predictBayesR3 can now also use a split prefix genotype file names.

·       During genotype read, bayesR3 now checks for duplicated entries (IDs)

·       Sped up the setting up of blocks in a multi-trait analysis.

·       Added the new command –parts and if set to 1 the genotype file name is considered a prefix/ (regular expression), otherwise the genotype file name is considered to represent a single file. Default value is 0.

·       Genotype file names are now be treated as prefix names, if the -parts switch is set to 1. When the genotype file is split into parts it can be read in parallel thereby speeding up the loading of a genotype file, which at times may take many hours.

 

To use a genotype prefix, pass bayesR3 via -genf the output prefix that was used to split the original genotype file into N parts as used by split:

 

o   zcat subSet4e4.txt.gz | split - -l10000 subParts4e4

 

Note:

·        Only split non-zipped genotype files.

·        The prefix should be unique with respect to split files.

 

For a genotype file containing 65,000 records/lines the above split command will generate the following 7 files:

 

subParts4e4aa subParts4e4ab subParts4e4ac subParts4e4ad subParts4e4ae subParts4e4af subParts4e4ag

 

Each file will contain10,000 records/lines except for the last file (subParts4e4ag), which will contain only 5,000 records/lines.

 

·       Genotype values outside the range 0 to 2 will now cause bayesR3 to throw an error.

·       Pedigree files are now allowed to have more than 3 columns, but only the first 3 columns are interpreted as animal ID, sire ID and dam ID, and in that order.

 

Update to Saturday, Tuesday, September 7, 2021

 

·       Fixed several bugs

·       Added command option plusAlpha

·       Reimplemented the dropping of SNPs. Dropping of SNPs occur only during burn in. The drop parameter is used specify to bayesR3 to drop SNPs from analysis that are consistently not being included in the bayesR3 model. The drop parameter takes 1 or 2 comma separated values. Default value is NA, which is used to specify no dropping.

 

For example:

 

-drop 100

 

Specifies that during burn in, a SNP will be dropped from analysis if in the last 100 iterations it was not included in the model. In this case dropping can only occur on and after the 100th iteration. 

 

-drop 100,200

 

Specifies that during burn in, a SNP will be dropped from analysis if in the previous 100 iterations it was not included in the model. In this case dropping starts at the 200th iteration.

 

-drop NA

 

Specifies no dropping.

·       predictBayesR3: fixed bug/feature that the genotype and phenotype files need to have the same records when using a reference file. Now only the IDs in the phenotype file not included in the reference file need to exist in the genotype file therefore the genotype file can contain extra records not defined in the genotype file.

·       Added a new bayesR3 command option “-n”, which is used to specify an integer number of inner-cycles, as opposed to the current method of setting inner-cycle number to equal the block size.  Lowest value allowed is 1, if specified otherwise “-n NA” or “-n -1” turns the option off and it is off, without specification, by default.

o   Note: this only changes the number of inner cycles, and how the inner and outer cycle mix to maintain the same number of required iteration and burn-in values specified in a parameter file

·       Fixed bug of bayesR3 crashing when certain parameters in the parameter were not defined or missing from the parameter file.

              

Update to Monday, January 25, 2021

 

·                 Corrected overflow problem for the reporting of the number of SNPs in class distributions.

 

Update to Wednesday, September 30, 2020

 

·                 Fixed issue with bayesR3 not computing the average inclusion probabilities (Q1 and Q2) in a multi-trait analysis across the chains. This is the result that ends up in the aveEffects file  as specified in see Table 9.

 

 

Updates to Thursday, September 24, 2020 (release date)

 

 

·                 A “Common errors encountered” section has been added to bayesR3’s documentation pdf.

·                 Removed the prior previously added in the estimation of Va. It was found on average to reduce prediction accuracy slightly.

·                 Added the ability for bayesR3 to incorporate family structure using a GRM (genomic relationship matrix) as described in its documentation pdf.

·                 A slight improvement in the average predication accuracy of bayesR3, was achieved by accumulating each SNP value directly after their sampling event during post-burn in. This is opposed to the previous strategy of collecting SNP effects during post-burn in at the end-of-each outer cycle.

·                 Fixed the error with the reported Vp value(s) in the log and model files, that was caused by dividing it wrongly by the number of post-burnin outer-cycles.

·                 Removed the artificial lower limit of 0.0002 imposed on the user’s specified minor allele frequency (MAF). It can now be any value greater than zero but less than or equal to 0.49.  

 

Updates to Tuesday, September 1, 2020 (release date)

 

·       Added a change log section at the end of the appendix section of the bayesR3 documentation

·       Finally managed to fix the Linux problem of core dumping. Fingers crossed

·       Added an extra output file when doing multi-chain analysis. In a multi-chain analysis, the SNP effects and their distribution proportions from each chain are collected averaged and stored with the other output files, but with the suffix aveEffects. The SNP effects reported in this file will be stored along with their chain variances and will be placed next to the effects in a column titled VB for a single trait analysis and for a multi trait analysis they are identified by VB.1,…, VB.n where n is the number of  traits analyzed:

·       Improved the speed of inputting files such as fixed effects, genotype, and phenotype files. The speed improvement comes about not by faster file reading but by not having to reorder the rows in each input matrix to match up across the various inputs.

·       In bayesR3, moved the reading of the fixed effects file, if passed, before the reading of the genotypes. This saves time when reporting errors to the user if there are problems, such as file formatting issues.

·       Added a prior to the calculation of the SNP effects variance that gets reported as Va. This is only active if DAV is set to 1. The prior uses the proportions from the parameter file, or command line:

 

-pi 0.94,0.049,0.01,0.001

 

to estimate the number of expected SNPs that should fall into the model. This in turn makes bayesR3 sensitive to these initial values. Therefore, for genotypes of 600K or larger, consider using:

 

-pi 0.994,0.0055,0.00049,0.00001 

 

·       predictBayesR3 now responds to the log file command -L. If -L 1 is passed or set in the parameter file, predictBayesR3 will append its output results (R^2 and slope) to the log file created by bayesR3.  If such a file doesn’t exist, then it will create it according to the prefix and path values set in the parameter file or passed on the command line.

·       Fixed the problem with bayesR3 and predictBayesR3 of ignoring user specified seed values in the parameter file or passed on the command line.  As only a single set of seed values can be specified then for a multi-chain analysis, the specified seed values will be divided into equal sized (if possible) seed sets for each chain. Therefore, in a multi chain analysis the number of seeds must be equal or greater than the number of chains specified.

·       Added command input validation. Previously, bayesR3/predictBayesR3 command and command values from parameter files or specified on the command line were accepted without any checking. Now they are checked, and any entered command is not in the set of valid commands an error is reported and the program stops.

·       Extended the accuracy of calculating the association probabilities in a multi-trait bayesR3 analysis. Previously, multi-trait analysis was limited to around at most 200 traits per analysis. Now bayesR3 can handle correctly at least 4608 traits (that is 23-fold improvement in the power of a multi-trait analysis).

·       Added the use of validation sets (-valid <filename>) in conjunction with the use of a reference (-ref <filename) set.

o   A validation set is only used by predictBayesR3. The validation set defines a set of records that are included into predictBayesR3’s prediction analysis, as opposed to just using a reference set, which specifies which records not to include in the prediction. Note if both reference and validation files are specified in a parameter file then bayesR3 uses the reference set, while predictBayesR3 uses only the validation set. Either or both can be set to NA.

·       Validation and reference files can now contain multiple columns. However, only the first column is used and is expected to contain the record IDs.

·       Fixed bug in the computing of fixed effects

·       Fixed minor bug with computing the Dirichlet probabilities
